description: Two-person sibling team. Between us we bring mechanical design, CAD, 3D printing, and electronics, along with programming from years of competitive robotics. We’re set as a pair for this one, but we’re always happy to swap ideas with other teams during the weekend.
summary:
LUNI (Lunar Utility for Navigational Intelligence) is a web app that answers one question fast: can this mission land here, at this time? You pick a landing site on the Moon and a landing time, and LUNI gives a plain GO or NO-GO for power and for a direct link to Earth, with the reason, countdowns to sunset and Earth set, and ways out of a NO-GO: the next landing window or a better spot nearby.

It addresses the challenge directly. It compares sites and dates quickly, shows the Sun and Earth against the real terrain skyline, and is readable by a planner, a teacher or a curious visitor. Every number is computed from NASA data (SPICE, LRO LOLA, LRO Diviner), and it matches NASA JPL Horizons to 0.0007°.

It matters because a launch slip or a few hundred meters can turn a workable landing into a dead lander.

LUNI won the Best Use of Data award at our local judging. Five people who had never seen it took its built-in six-task test, and four of the five scored 6 of 6. It comes with a 45-minute classroom lesson that teachers reviewed. The lesson and the story of how LUNI was built are at https://galileoleosolis.github.io/LUNI/about/
details:
**What it does**

- **The answer.** For a site, a landing time and a set of mission needs (mission length, how long the lander can sit in the dark, how much Earth link it needs, how steep the ground may be), LUNI says GO or NO-GO and why. A NO-GO comes with buttons that get to a GO.

- **The view from the site.** The skyline all the way round, drawn from elevation data, with the Sun, the Earth in its real phase, and where each will go over the next 3 days. Eclipses (Earth passing in front of the Sun) are detected and flagged.

- **Mission plan, operations and mission windows.** A 30-day timeline with a slider for any moment of the mission; an operations view that lays the mission out as stretches in order (power and link, power only, on battery, eclipse); and every good landing day for the next 12 months.

- **Where water ice could last.** A map layer and a data card row from NASA's Diviner Polar Resource Product: how deep below the surface water ice would stay frozen, at both poles.

- **Energy.** An hour-by-hour power budget for the plan: what a solar panel collects (NASA's measured sunlight strength, 1,361 W per square meter, times LUNI's own share of the Sun's disc in view each hour), what the lander uses, and the battery needed to ride out every stretch without enough Sun. The panel size, its efficiency and the lander's power use are the user's to set.

- **Before and after.** When the Best Site Finder moves the site or Next Landing Window moves the date, a box puts the original plan next to the new one: verdict, sunlight, time without Sun, Earth link and energy, with the change in each and a button to go back. Two listed sites can be put side by side the same way.

- **Solar panel placement.** In the Best Site Finder, give a distance from the lander and a number of panels; LUNI marks the sunniest squares within that distance and adds up the energy they would collect.

- **All sites side by side.** Every site in the list carries a green or red dot for the landing time on screen, and a ranked table shows how many good landing days each site has. Any latitude and longitude can be typed in.

- **Best Site Finder.** LUNI checks a grid of points around the site, out to 60 km away, and marks the best one that meets the needs. The skylines are computed on the graphics chip when one is available, and each run first checks itself against the processor.

- **Moon map with layers.** The 3D Moon with elevation, slope, sunlight, Earth link and temperature for the whole Moon, at finer detail around both poles, where permanent shadow is mapped as well. Green is good, red is bad, and each layer names its data source. A data profile card gives every layer's value at any point. The layers can be blended with your own weights into one score, and that mix can pick the best point in the scan.

- **Mission history.** Six real landings since 2023 (Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, IM-1, Chang'e 6, Blue Ghost Mission 1, IM-2) side by side, each loadable into the main screen at its real date and hour.

- **For every skill level.** A simple view by default with every tool one press away, a guided tutorial that lights up one part of the screen at a time, plain-language labels, typed or spoken commands (ASK LUNI), a 3D first-person view from the surface, a comparison of the site with a place on Earth, and a link that reopens LUNI on the exact same question.

**How it works**

LUNI is a static web page with no server. Sun and Earth directions come from a table built from NASA SPICE (DE440) for 2023 to 2035, in the same Moon-fixed frame as the elevation maps. For each site LUNI builds the terrain skyline from LRO LOLA elevation and compares the Sun's disc and the Earth with it, hour by hour. "Sun" means at least half of the Sun's disc is in view from 2 m above the ground. The map layers were worked out the same way: for 1.26 million points around each pole (480 m squares, every 6 hours over 2023 to 2035) and for about a million quarter-degree squares over the rest of the Moon. Temperatures are NASA's own Diviner values, only re-gridded.

**How we know it is right**

- Sun and Earth positions agree with NASA JPL Horizons within 0.0007° across 1,110 values at 6 sites. The app links to NASA's own answer for whatever is on screen.

- Blue Ghost Mission 1: LUNI works out 347 hours of daylight after touchdown; Firefly reported 346. LUNI puts the 14 March 2025 eclipse at 05:01 to 09:51 UTC with the Sun fully hidden from 06:18; the lander's pictures give about 05:30, 06:18 and 09:52.

- LUNI's polar map layers agree with NASA's own polar maps from the LRO LOLA team: sunlight correlates at 0.99 at both poles with an average gap under 2 points, and "never sunlit" gives the same answer as NASA's permanently shadowed regions map in 99.1% of the 1.26 million squares at the south pole and 98.9% at the north pole.

- Chandrayaan-3: LUNI's sunset is 4 September 2023, the day the lander was put to sleep ahead of the lunar night.

- The app lists what it does not model: the landing itself, rocks and craters smaller than a map pixel, panel direction, lander tilt, antennas and relay satellites.

**Benefits and what we hope to achieve**

A planner can re-check a site after a schedule slip in seconds instead of moving between several tools. A teacher or student can see why the Moon's south pole is hard: a Sun that stays within a few degrees of the horizon near the pole, sunsets that take hours, and craters that never see sunlight next to ridges that almost always do. We hope LUNI is useful as a first look before detailed analysis, and as a way for anyone to explore real mission conditions.

We tested it with people and changed it after every round. Inside the team, five rounds took the score on LUNI's built-in six-task test from 2 of 6 to 6 of 6. Then five people who had never seen LUNI, friends and family, took the test: four of the five scored 6 of 6, in 8 to 13 minutes, and what their reports showed was built the same evening.

LUNI also comes with a 45-minute classroom lesson in which students plan their own Moon landing: a worksheet with a worked example, an answer key, and a checklist for a teacher who has never taught science. Teachers reviewed it and it was rewritten around their feedback. One of them wrote: "It's really incredible, can't wait to see where this goes." The lesson is at https://galileoleosolis.github.io/LUNI/about/

At our local judging, LUNI won the Best Use of Data award.

**Tools**

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no build step), WebGL2, Web Workers, the Web Speech API, three.js for the 3D views; Python with NumPy and SpiceyPy to prepare the NASA data; Node.js for the checks; Playwright for layout checks; GitHub Pages for hosting; an optional link to OpenSpace. The code was written with an AI assistant (see Use of SI).
